title: Absorption by Roots
tagline: Diffusion, osmosis, the state of the cell sap, and how water and minerals actually get into a root.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every physical process, cell state and measurement below is standard plant physiology. Diffusion pressure deficit is expressed in the classical form DPD equals osmotic pressure minus turgor pressure. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A root absorbs water not because it is thirsty but because of the physical properties of water itself, and this chapter builds the explanation from first principles. It defines diffusion, osmosis and the direction water moves, then introduces the concept that decides everything else — diffusion pressure deficit, the net pull a solution exerts on water. With that in place it follows a root hair absorbing by osmosis, examines what happens to a cell in solutions of different strengths — turgid, flaccid, plasmolysed and deplasmolysed — and covers the two supporting phenomena, imbibition and root pressure, before explaining why mineral salts need a different, energy-requiring mechanism altogether.

facts.label: Water movement

facts.value: Osmotic pressure minus turgor pressure — the net suction of a solution

learningOutcomes: Define diffusion and osmosis and state the direction water moves across a selectively permeable membrane.
Explain diffusion pressure deficit and use it to predict the direction of water movement between two solutions.
Describe the absorption of water by a root hair and account for turgidity, flaccidity, plasmolysis and deplasmolysis.
Distinguish osmosis from active transport and explain why mineral salts require energy to enter the root.

learn.title: Diffusion, osmosis and diffusion pressure deficit

blocks.text: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, continuing until the particles are evenly distributed and dynamic equilibrium is reached. It is a physical process that needs no energy from the cell, it speeds up with temperature, and it can occur in gases and liquids alike — the scent of a flower spreading across a room is diffusion. Osmosis is the special case that governs plant water relations: it is the movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration. In plant cells the membrane is the cell membrane, which lets water through freely but blocks most dissolved solutes, so the practical consequence is that water moves towards the more concentrated solution. The cell's tendency to take in water depends on the balance between the osmotic pressure, which draws water in, and the turgor pressure of the swollen wall pushing back — and the difference between them is the diffusion pressure deficit, which is the net pull the cell can exert.

items.meaning: Net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration until equilibrium is reached; requires no energy.
Movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from a weaker to a more concentrated solution.
A membrane that allows some substances to pass but not others — here, water but not the solute.
The pressure a solution would develop if it were separated from pure water by a membrane; greater in a stronger solution.
The pressure of the swollen protoplast pushing outward against the cell wall in a turgid cell.
OP minus TP; the net suction force a solution or cell has for water. Also called suction force.
The tendency of water to move; pure water at atmospheric pressure has the highest possible value.

blocks.caption: Solutions and the direction of water movement

items: DPD = osmotic pressure minus turgor pressure, so a turgid cell with TP equal to OP has a DPD of zero and takes in no more water.
Water always moves from lower DPD to higher DPD, which is the statement that lets you predict the direction of movement.
In a flaccid cell the turgor pressure falls to zero, so DPD equals osmotic pressure and the cell can still take in water.
Diffusion is physical and needs no energy; active transport needs energy and can move a solute against its gradient.
Osmosis requires a selectively permeable membrane — without one it is simply diffusion.
A cell in pure water cannot burst because the wall pushes back with increasing force as the cell swells.
The greater the concentration difference across the membrane, the faster the rate of osmosis.
DPD is greatest in a cell with high osmotic pressure and no turgor pressure, that is, a plasmolysed cell.

items.text: Place a plant cell in a strong sugar solution and water leaves the protoplast, so the DPD inside rises above that outside and the protoplast eventually pulls away from the cell wall.
items.note: The wall stays in shape while the membrane shrinks — that separation is plasmolysis.

items.text: A root hair cell maintains a very concentrated cell sap, so its DPD is always higher than that of the soil water, and water flows in continuously as long as the sap stays concentrated.
items.note: The root does not create the pull; the concentration difference does.

learn.title: How a root hair absorbs water and minerals

blocks.text: A root hair is not a separate cell but a long tubular extension of one cell of the epidermis, and its design is entirely about surface area. It is long, thin-walled and filled with cell sap whose dissolved salts give it a high osmotic pressure and therefore a high diffusion pressure deficit relative to the soil water. Water in the soil film enters the hair across the cell membrane by osmosis, down the water potential gradient, and the hair's shape gives an enormous absorbing surface without the root having to increase greatly in diameter. Once inside, water crosses the cortex by osmosis from cell to cell and also through the non-living cell walls and intercellular spaces in what is called the apoplastic route, until it reaches the endodermis. There the Casparian strip forces it to cross a membrane, which is the checkpoint that lets the plant control what enters the vascular tissue. Minerals, by contrast, cannot enter by osmosis because they are moving towards a higher concentration inside the cell; they are carried across by active transport, using energy from respiration, and this is why roots need oxygen.

blocks.caption: Water by osmosis against minerals by active transport
rows: Osmosis across a selectively permeable membrane

Down the water potential gradient, to the more concentrated side
Often against the concentration gradient, into the cell
None; supplied by the gradient itself
Yes — ATP from respiration in the root

Directly — no oxygen means no respiration and no uptake
The great bulk of what enters the root

items: A root hair may be up to several millimetres long — enormous for a single epidermal cell — purely to increase surface area.
The wall of a root hair is very thin and permeable, shortening the distance water must cross.
Cell sap with a high concentration of dissolved salts gives the hair a high DPD, which is what draws water in.
The Casparian strip in the endodermis is waxy and waterproof, blocking the wall pathway and forcing water through a membrane.
The cortex of a root has plenty of intercellular spaces, which is why air is essential for root function and waterlogging is damaging.
Mineral uptake is selective: a plant fed a solution lacking one ion will show a deficiency even when every other ion is abundant.
Osmosis explains water entry but cannot explain entry of minerals against a gradient.
The root hair is temporary — it dies as the root tip matures and new hairs form behind the growing region.

items.text: A plant grown in a complete nutrient solution thrives, while one given the same solution with the nitrogen removed turns pale and stunted, even though water uptake continues normally.
items.note: Water and minerals use different mechanisms, so one can proceed while the other fails.

items.text: Seedlings raised in waterlogged sand die although the sand is wet, because the roots cannot obtain the oxygen needed to generate the ATP for active transport.
items.note: Water is abundant, yet the plant starves for lack of oxygen.

blocks.text: The state of a plant cell in a given solution is determined by which way the water moves, and each state has a name that must be used precisely. When a cell is placed in pure water or a very dilute solution, water enters faster than it leaves, the vacuole swells, and the protoplast presses firmly against the cell wall; the cell is then turgid, and the outward push it makes is the turgor pressure. Turgidity is what keeps a soft plant upright, since herbaceous plants have no skeleton. When the surrounding solution is more concentrated than the cell sap, water leaves the cell, the vacuole shrinks and the protoplast becomes loose inside the wall — the cell is flaccid, and the turgor pressure falls to zero. If water loss continues, the protoplast actually shrinks away from the cell wall and the cell is plasmolysed. Plasmolysis is reversible: returning the cell to pure water allows water to re-enter, the protoplast swells back against the wall and the cell is deplasmolysed. The process fails permanently if the cell is left plasmolysed too long, because the membrane is damaged and cannot regain its selective permeability.

blocks.caption: The four states of a plant cell
rows: Protoplast pressed firmly against the wall
Protoplast just touching the wall, no push
Protoplast shrunk away from the wall
Protoplast swollen against the wall again
Membrane bursts, no wall to resist

items: Turgor pressure is maximum in a turgid cell, where TP equals OP and so DPD becomes zero.
A flaccid cell has TP of zero, which is why it has a DPD equal to its full osmotic pressure.
Plasmolysis is the shrinking of the protoplast away from the cell wall, and it only happens when the cell is living.
Deplasmolysis is the recovery of a plasmolysed cell when placed in pure water or a very dilute solution.
Plasmolysis is permanent if prolonged, because the membrane loses its selective permeability and the cell dies.
An animal cell in pure water bursts because it has no wall to restrain it; a plant cell merely becomes turgid.
Wilting of a whole plant corresponds to flaccidity in its mesophyll cells as the vacuoles lose water.
Plasmolysis can be observed directly by placing onion epidermis in a strong salt solution and viewing it under a microscope.

items.text: A wilted cut stem placed in water recovers within hours as its cells move from flaccid back to turgid — deplasmolysis at the scale of a whole plant.
items.note: The visible recovery is the sum of countless individual cells regaining turgor.

items.text: Onion epidermis in concentrated salt solution shows the purple protoplast drawing back from the clear wall; transferring the same strip to pure water makes it swell back within minutes.
items.note: The reversibility of the observation is what makes it a clean demonstration.

learn.title: Imbibition, root pressure and the ascent of water

blocks.text: Imbibition is the absorption of water by a solid — a dry material — causing it to swell, and it is a special case of adsorption rather than osmosis, because there is often no membrane and no true solution involved. It nonetheless explains several important things: dry seeds take up water by imbibition and swell so forcefully that they can split a hard seed coat or even crack a laboratory container; the water drawn into the cell walls of the root is held there by the same adsorptive forces; and the adhesion of water to the cellulose of the xylem walls helps pull the water column upwards. Root pressure is the positive pressure that builds in the root and pushes xylem sap upwards, and it is most easily observed as guttation — droplets of sap exuded from the leaf edges at night, when transpiration is low but absorption continues. Root pressure can raise a column of sap in a stump but is far too weak to account for water reaching the top of a tall tree, so it assists the initial rise only; the main pull comes from transpiration at the leaves.

items.meaning: Absorption of water by a solid such as a dry seed or cellulose, causing swelling; an adsorption phenomenon.
Loss of liquid water as droplets from hydathodes at the leaf margin when transpiration is low and root pressure is high.
The positive pressure built up in the root that pushes xylem sap upward.
Attraction between like water molecules, which holds the xylem water column together.
Attraction of water molecules to the cellulose of the xylem wall, helping support the column.
The suction created at the leaf surfaces as water evaporates, which pulls the whole water column upward.

items: Imbibition explains why a dry seed swells and why its testa splits during the very first stage of germination.
Seed coats and laboratory containers have both been cracked by the immense pressure of imbibition in dry material.
Root pressure is generated by the active transport of minerals into the xylem, which lowers water potential and draws water in by osmosis.
Guttation is the visible evidence of root pressure, and it is liquid sap rather than water vapour, unlike transpiration.
Root pressure is strongest in small herbaceous plants and in spring when absorption is active and transpiration is low.
Water in the xylem is under tension, which is why a cut shoot placed in water will not readily bubble when first cut.
Cohesion between water molecules keeps the xylem column continuous over many metres without it breaking.
Adhesion to the xylem walls counteracts gravity and helps hold the column up between the vessel elements.
Most water absorbed — well over ninety per cent — is lost again by transpiration rather than used in photosynthesis.

items.text: Soak a dry pea and its seed coat splits within a day although nothing has cut it; the swelling of the cotyledons by imbibition is strong enough to tear the testa at the micropyle.
items.note: No membrane and no osmosis are involved — the water is adsorbed to the dry colloids.

items.text: On a cool, humid morning a strawberry leaf shows clear droplets along its serrated edge, which is guttation from hydathodes driven by root pressure when transpiration cannot take the water away.
items.note: Distinguish it from dew: guttation comes from inside the leaf and appears at the margin.

keyPoints: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration until equilibrium, and needs no energy.
Osmosis is water movement through a selectively permeable membrane from a weaker to a more concentrated solution.
DPD = osmotic pressure minus turgor pressure; water moves from lower DPD to higher DPD.
A turgid cell has turgor pressure equal to osmotic pressure, so its DPD is zero and it takes in no more water.
A root hair is an extension of one epidermal cell with a thin wall, a large surface and concentrated cell sap.
Water enters the root by osmosis, but minerals enter by active transport and need ATP from respiration.
The Casparian strip of the endodermis blocks the wall pathway and forces water to cross a membrane.
Plasmolysis is the shrinking of the protoplast from the wall in a strong solution; deplasmolysis is its recovery in pure water.
Imbibition is water absorption by a dry solid, which swells the seed and splits its coat.
Root pressure causes guttation but is far too weak to lift water to the top of a tall tree — transpiration pull does that.
examFocus: Always give the direction of water movement with its reason — from lower DPD to higher DPD — because a name without a direction loses the mark.
Turgid, flaccid and plasmolysed must each be tied to the state of the protoplast against the wall and to the value of turgor pressure.
Imbibition is not osmosis: it is adsorption by a solid, and calling it osmosis loses the mark outright.
Guttation and transpiration are commonly contrasted, so state the substance lost, the time of day and the driving force for each.
For mineral absorption, quote active transport and the need for energy from respiration; osmosis cannot move an ion against its gradient.

Osmotic pressure minus turgor pressure; the net suction a solution has for water.
Outward pressure of the swollen protoplast against the cell wall.
Shrinking of the protoplast away from the cell wall in a hypertonic solution.
Recovery of a plasmolysed cell when placed in pure water.
Absorption of water by a dry solid causing swelling.
Positive pressure in the root that pushes xylem sap upward.
Movement of a substance against its concentration gradient using energy from respiration.

questions.prompt: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens to its diffusion pressure deficit and why?
options: It rises, because osmotic pressure increases
It falls to zero, because turgor pressure rises to equal osmotic pressure
It stays the same, because water moves both ways equally
It rises, because water leaves the cell
questions.answer: It falls to zero, because turgor pressure rises to equal osmotic pressure
questions.explanation: Water enters the cell by osmosis, the vacuole swells and the protoplast presses against the wall, so turgor pressure increases. Since DPD equals osmotic pressure minus turgor pressure, the rising turgor pressure reduces DPD until, in a fully turgid cell, turgor pressure equals osmotic pressure and DPD becomes zero, at which point no further water enters.
questions.commonMistake: Saying DPD rises because water enters. DPD is a net suction; filling the cell removes the suction rather than increasing it.

questions.prompt: Diffusion pressure deficit is calculated as __________ pressure minus __________ pressure, and water always moves from a lower DPD to a higher DPD.
questions.explanation: Osmotic pressure represents the solution's capacity to draw water in, while turgor pressure is the wall's outward push resisting that entry. The difference between them is the net suction, or diffusion pressure deficit, and water flows along this gradient — from the region of lower deficit to the region of higher deficit.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the subtraction. The formula is osmotic pressure minus turgor pressure; subtracting the other way gives a meaningless negative value for a turgid cell.

questions.prompt: Which condition correctly describes a plant cell that has been placed in a strong sugar solution?
options: Hypotonic outside, water entering, cell turgid
Hypertonic outside, water leaving, cell plasmolysed
Isotonic outside, no net movement, cell unchanged
Hypotonic outside, water leaving, cell flaccid
questions.answer: Hypertonic outside, water leaving, cell plasmolysed
questions.explanation: A strong sugar solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell sap, so it is hypertonic or outside. Water moves out of the cell down its own gradient, the vacuole shrinks and the protoplast pulls away from the wall, which is plasmolysis. A hypotonic solution outside would drive water in and make the cell turgid.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing hypertonic with hypotonic. Hyper means over or stronger, so the stronger solution is outside and water moves out of the cell.

questions.prompt: State three structural features of a root hair that make it efficient at absorbing water, and explain the function of each.
questions.answer: Its great length and tubular shape give a very large surface area relative to its volume, so a large area of membrane is available for water to cross in the same time. Its wall is extremely thin, which shortens the distance water must travel and so speeds up entry. Its cell sap is concentrated with dissolved salts, giving a high osmotic pressure and therefore a high diffusion pressure deficit relative to the soil water, which creates the gradient that draws water in by osmosis.
questions.explanation: Three features are required with a function attached to each: surface area from shape, speed from thinness, and direction from concentration. Describing the appearance without stating what it achieves earns only part of the credit, because the question is explicitly about efficiency.
questions.commonMistake: Calling the root hair a separate cell. It is an extension of one epidermal cell, and misidentifying it weakens the whole description.

questions.prompt: Describe what is meant by plasmolysis, explain how it is brought about, and state what happens when the plasmolysed cell is transferred to pure water.
questions.answer: Plasmolysis is the shrinking of the protoplast away from the cell wall when a living plant cell is placed in a solution more concentrated than its cell sap. Because the surrounding solution is hypertonic, water moves out of the cell by osmosis down the water potential gradient. The vacuole loses water and contracts, the protoplast loses volume, and since the wall no longer supports it from outside, the membrane draws inwards and separates from the wall, leaving a gap filled with the external solution. The cell is now plasmolysed and its turgor pressure is zero. If the cell is then transferred to pure water, water re-enters by osmosis, the vacuole swells, the protoplast expands and presses against the wall again, and the cell becomes deplasmolysed and then turgid. If plasmolysis is prolonged, however, the membrane loses its selective permeability and the cell cannot recover, so the process is only reversible for a limited time.
questions.explanation: The answer must give the state, the cause and the reversal, and should note the time limit on reversibility since that is what distinguishes temporary from fatal plasmolysis. Tracing water out and then back in shows the underlying mechanism rather than merely naming the phenomenon.
questions.commonMistake: Describing plasmolysis as the cell collapsing or bursting. The wall keeps its shape; only the protoplast shrinks away from it.

questions.prompt: Why must a root take in oxygen in order to absorb mineral salts from the soil?
options: Because oxygen is a raw material needed to build amino acids in the root
Because mineral ions are absorbed by active transport, which requires energy released during aerobic respiration
Because oxygen helps the cell membrane become fully permeable to minerals
Because minerals dissolve in oxygen before they can enter the root hair
questions.answer: Because mineral ions are absorbed by active transport, which requires energy released during aerobic respiration
questions.explanation: Mineral ions are taken up against their concentration gradient, from a weaker soil solution into a cell already rich in ions. Moving a substance against a gradient cannot be done by osmosis and requires energy, which the root obtains as ATP from aerobic respiration. Without oxygen there is no aerobic respiration, no ATP, and no mineral uptake — which is why waterlogged roots fail.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking oxygen is used to make the minerals. Oxygen is needed for energy, not as a chemical reactant in uptake.

questions.prompt: A plant is growing in soil that is watered generously every day, and the leaves begin to wilt although the soil is visibly wet. Suggest an explanation, name the condition of the mesophyll cells, describe what you would expect to see under a microscope if you examined those cells, and state one measure that should restore the plant.
questions.answer: Generous watering has filled the air spaces between soil particles with water, so oxygen can no longer reach the roots. Without oxygen the roots cannot respire aerobically, so they produce little ATP and cannot carry out the active transport of minerals against their concentration gradient. Mineral uptake falls, the concentration of the cell sap in the root and then in the shoot is not maintained, and the plant can no longer draw water from the soil by osmosis even though water is abundant — so the leaves lose water by transpiration faster than they receive it and the plant wilts. The mesophyll cells are flaccid: their vacuoles have lost water, the protoplasts rest against the walls without pushing, and turgor pressure has fallen to zero. Under the microscope the cells would show shrunken vacuoles and no outward pressure on the wall, though the protoplasts would not yet have separated from it. If the condition continues the cells would become plasmolysed, with the protoplast pulling right away from the wall. Restoring the plant requires improving drainage and allowing the soil to dry between waterings so that oxygen returns to the root zone.
questions.explanation: The apparent paradox — wet soil yet wilting — must be resolved through oxygen rather than water, and the chain runs oxygen to respiration to active transport to mineral uptake to osmosis. Naming the cell state, describing the microscopic appearance and giving a corrective measure each carry their own marks, so all four parts must be answered.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the plant is overwatered and stopping. The mechanism — oxygen exclusion shutting down active transport, which then breaks the osmotic gradient — is what earns the marks.

questions.prompt: What is imbibition, and how does it explain the splitting of a seed coat during germination?
questions.answer: Imbibition is the absorption of water by a dry solid material, causing it to swell. It is an adsorption process in which water molecules are attracted to the colloidal substances of the dry material, and it does not require a membrane or a solution. During germination the dry seed takes up water by imbibition before any osmosis can occur, and as the cotyledons and embryo swell, the pressure they exert on the rigid testa becomes great enough to split it, usually at the micropyle, allowing the radicle to emerge.
questions.explanation: Both parts are needed: what imbibition is, and how the swelling produces a physical force. It is worth stating explicitly that imbibition precedes osmosis, because the dry seed cannot carry out osmosis until water has already been taken up by adsorption.
questions.commonMistake: Calling imbibition osmosis. There is no selectively permeable membrane and no solution in a dry seed, so it is adsorption, not osmosis.

questions.prompt: Which observation is direct evidence that root pressure is operating in a plant?
options: Wilting of the leaves on a hot afternoon
Guttation droplets at the leaf margin on a cool night
Rapid transpiration from the stomata in bright sunlight
Swelling of a dry seed placed in water
questions.answer: Guttation droplets at the leaf margin on a cool night
questions.explanation: Guttation is the exudation of liquid sap from hydathodes at the edge of the leaf, and it happens when absorption by the roots continues while transpiration is minimal, so root pressure pushes the xylem sap up and out. Wilting indicates water loss exceeding uptake, transpiration is the evaporative loss itself, and seed swelling is imbibition rather than any root process.
questions.commonMistake: Mistaking dew for guttation. Dew condenses from the air onto the leaf surface, whereas guttation comes from within through hydathodes.

questions.prompt: When a plant cell is placed in a solution stronger than its cell sap, water leaves by __________ and the cell becomes __________ before the protoplast finally separates from the cell wall.
questions.explanation: Water always moves across the selectively permeable membrane towards the more concentrated solution, so a strong external solution draws water out of the cell by osmosis. The first consequence of that water loss is flaccidity, in which turgor pressure falls to zero and the protoplast merely rests against the wall; only with further loss does the protoplast pull away and the cell become plasmolysed.
questions.commonMistake: Jumping straight to plasmolysed. Flaccidity is the intermediate state in which the protoplast still touches the wall.

questions.prompt: Explain why root pressure cannot be the main force lifting water to the top of a tall tree, and describe the mechanism that does account for it.
questions.answer: Root pressure is a positive push generated at the base of the plant, and while it can raise a column of sap a short distance, it is far too weak to lift water the many metres required by a tall tree — the resistance in the narrow xylem and the weight of the water column overcome it long before the top is reached. Root pressure is also absent from a tree that has lost its roots or is under rapid transpiration, yet water still rises, which shows it cannot be the main mechanism. The force that does account for the ascent is the transpiration pull: as water evaporates from the mesophyll surfaces, water potential in those cells falls, so water is drawn from adjacent cells and ultimately from the xylem, and a continuous tension is transmitted down the whole column to the roots. Because water molecules cohere strongly with one another and adhere to the xylem walls, the column does not break under tension, and this evaporation-driven pull at the leaves lifts the water from below.
questions.explanation: The first half must argue from strength and from evidence — the mechanism operates even without root pressure — and the second half must name transpiration pull and explain the two properties, cohesion and adhesion, that let a continuous column be pulled upwards without cavitation.
questions.commonMistake: Naming transpiration pull without cohesion. Cohesion is what allows the tension to be transmitted; without it the column would simply break.
